detail:
Mayo Clinic's gastroparesis guidance starts with how food is eaten: smaller, more frequent meals; foods low in fat and in hard-to-digest fiber; soft or liquid foods when symptoms are severe; and, for people with diabetes, attention to blood glucose, since high glucose itself slows stomach emptying. Treatment does not cure gastroparesis, which is usually chronic and relapsing, so the goal is controlling symptom severity.

When diet is not enough, clinicians may use medicines: metoclopramide is the only FDA-approved prokinetic for gastroparesis, and anti-nausea medicines are common additions. Mayo describes procedures such as gastric electrical stimulation or pylorus-directed treatment as options for severe, refractory cases at specialized centers.

Talk to your doctor before starting or changing any medication.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material.
summary: Mayo Clinic describes dietary change as the first step in gastroparesis care: smaller, more frequent meals that are low in fat and fiber and easy to digest, with medicines and procedures reserved for more severe cases.
takeaways: small, frequent meals are easier for the stomach to empty
low-fat, low-fiber foods are usually emphasized
metoclopramide is the only fda-approved stomach-emptying medicine
diet changes and medicines belong in a plan with your doctor or dietitian
title: Managing gastroparesis: small meals first
